lessons.title: Residential Risks: Project Delays, Oversupply and Slow Exits

children.text: Around 2010, tens of thousands of families in Noida and Greater Noida booked flats with Jaypee and Amrapali, two of the region's best-known developers. Many were promised possession within three or four years. Instead they spent the next decade paying rent and EMIs at the same time, filing cases, and waiting for courts to decide who would finish their homes. Those buyers did not lose money because property prices fell. They lost it because the specific risks of residential property, which rarely appear in a brochure, all arrived at once.

body.text: The biggest residential risks are not about price. They are about whether the flat gets built, whether too many similar flats get built around it, and whether you can sell when you need the money.

children.text: Risk 1: Project Delays and Stalled Projects

markDefs.definition: Interest-only payments on the portion of a home loan disbursed during construction. Full EMIs covering principal start only after the final disbursement or possession.

children.text: When you buy an under-construction flat, you are lending money to a developer with the flat as the promised repayment. If the developer diverts funds to buy land for the next project, runs out of cash or goes insolvent, construction slows or stops. Buyers are left paying
on their loans while also paying rent for the home they actually live in.

events.title: RERA becomes fully operational
events.description: New projects must register, disclose approvals and timelines, and park 70% of buyer money in a dedicated project account.

events.title: Jaypee Infratech admitted to insolvency
events.description: Around 20,000 homebuyers in Noida and Greater Noida are left waiting for delayed flats.

events.title: Homebuyers recognised as financial creditors
events.description: An amendment to the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code gives homebuyers a seat at the table when a developer goes insolvent.

events.title: Supreme Court acts on Amrapali
events.description: The court cancels Amrapali's RERA registrations and directs state-owned NBCC to complete the stalled projects.

events.title: SWAMIH Fund launched
events.description: A government-backed fund begins providing last-mile finance to complete stalled affordable and mid-income projects.

events.title: Suraksha Group plan approved for Jaypee
events.description: The insolvency tribunal approves a resolution plan to take over and complete Jaypee Infratech's projects.

events.title: SWAMIH Fund 2 announced
events.description: The Union Budget announces a second fund of ₹15,000 crore after the first completed around 50,000 homes.

children.text: RERA has made new projects much safer than those of the pre-2017 era. It does not make delays impossible, but it gives buyers real remedies.

stats.label: Buyer money ring-fenced

stats.label: Remedy for delay

body.text: The discount on an under-construction flat is not a bargain. It is payment for taking on the developer's completion risk. Before accepting it, check the developer's record of on-time delivery on its last five projects, visit those projects, and read the RERA portal's quarterly progress updates for the one you are buying.

markDefs.definition: Unsold housing stock in a market divided by the average number of units sold per month. It estimates how long it would take to clear existing supply at the current pace of sales.

children.text: Prices and rents are set locally. If developers launch thousands of similar 2BHKs in the same suburb, your flat competes with every one of them for tenants and buyers. Rents stay flat, vacancy rises and resale prices stall, even if the city as a whole is doing well. The quickest way to spot this risk is

body.caption: Property consultants often express the same idea as "years to sell". Lower is healthier for prices and rents.

children.text: Suppose a suburban micro-market has 18,000 unsold flats and sells about 600 a month. At that pace it would take 30 months, two and a half years, to clear existing stock, before a single new project launches. A buyer there has little pricing power as a seller and a lot of competition as a landlord. A micro-market with 12 months of inventory is a very different place to own a flat.

body.text: The suburbs with the heaviest supply are often the ones marketed hardest as "the next growth corridor". Heavy advertising, lots of cranes and aggressive launch offers can be signs of oversupply rather than demand.

children.text: You can sell a Nifty ETF on NSE in seconds through Zerodha. A flat takes months. You cannot sell 10% of it to raise cash for an emergency. And every sale involves a buyer who needs a loan sanction, a society NOC, and a trip to the sub-registrar. In a weak market, the time stretches and the negotiated price drops.

body.caption: What a typical resale really involves

cells: Asking price too high for current demand
Buyer backs out or renegotiates after inspection
Bank objects to missing documents or approvals
Your loan closure and document release
Delay in getting original title documents back from your bank

children.text: Selling also costs money: brokerage of around 1% to 2%, and capital gains tax on any profit. That is why the right question before buying is not "will this appreciate?" but "if I needed this money in 18 months, how would I get it out?"

body.caption: Other residential risks and how to reduce them

cells: Disputed ownership, missing occupancy certificate, no utility connections
Lawyer-led title search, encumbrance certificate, verify occupancy certificate
Inspect developer's older projects; use RERA's 5-year defect liability
Poor upkeep, disputes, unpaid dues, sudden special levies
Speak to existing residents; check society finances before buying resale
Floating EMIs rise, buyer demand falls
Borrow conservatively; stress-test EMI at 2 percentage points higher
One flat is most of your net worth
Size property as one part of a diversified portfolio

body.title: Calculate: Months of Inventory
body.prompt: A micro-market near Hyderabad's Outer Ring Road has 9,600 unsold flats. Over the past year, it has sold 4,800 flats. How many months of inventory does it have?
body.explanation: Monthly sales: 4,800 ÷ 12 = 400. Months of inventory: 9,600 ÷ 400 = 24 months, or two years of supply at the current pace of sales.

body.title: Fill in the Blank: RERA Escrow
body.textWithBlank: Under RERA, developers must deposit ___% of the money collected from buyers into a separate account for that project.
body.explanation: The 70% rule is meant to stop developers from diverting buyer money from one project to buy land or fund another.

body.title: Quick Check: Your Rights on Delay
body.question: A RERA-registered project misses its promised possession date by two years. What remedies does RERA give the buyer?
options: None, because delays are a normal business risk
Only a refund of the principal paid, with no interest
Withdraw with a refund plus interest, or stay in the project and receive interest for each month of delay
An automatic 10% discount on the flat price
body.explanation: RERA lets a buyer choose between exiting with a refund and interest, or continuing and receiving interest for every month of delay until possession. Actually collecting it can still take time and effort through the state RERA authority.

body.title: Scenario: Wait or Walk Away?
body.scenario: Rohit booked an under-construction 2BHK in Greater Noida West for ₹60 lakh. The bank has disbursed ₹50 lakh of his loan at 8.5%, so he pays pre-EMI, while also paying ₹25,000 a month in rent. The project is RERA-registered and possession is already 12 months late. The developer now says it needs another 36 months. The RERA portal shows construction progress has barely moved in two quarters.
body.prompt: What will waiting 36 more months cost Rohit, and what should he consider?
body.modelAnswer: Pre-EMI on ₹50 lakh at 8.5% is ₹50 lakh × 8.5% ÷ 12 = about ₹35,417 a month. Add ₹25,000 rent and he spends about ₹60,417 a month, or roughly ₹21.75 lakh over 36 months, with no certainty the flat will be delivered even then. Stalled quarterly progress is a serious warning sign. He should check the developer's finances and other projects, talk to other buyers, and file a complaint with the UP RERA authority. RERA lets him either withdraw and claim a refund with interest, or stay and claim interest for the delay. If the developer looks financially stressed, withdrawing early, ideally together with other buyers, may protect more of his money than waiting. If the project is close to completion and the developer is sound, staying and claiming delay interest may be better.

cards.definition: Interest-only payments on the disbursed part of a home loan during construction.
A local authority certificate confirming a building is complete as per approvals and fit to occupy.
Unsold units divided by average monthly sales; how long current supply takes to clear.
The separate account where developers must deposit 70% of buyer money for that project.
Five years from possession during which the developer must fix structural defects under RERA.
A government-backed fund that provides last-mile finance to complete stalled housing projects.

points: Under-construction flats carry completion risk, and buyers can end up paying pre-EMI and rent at the same time for years.
RERA ring-fences 70% of buyer money, gives five years of structural defect liability, and lets buyers claim a refund or delay interest.
The discount on under-construction property is payment for risk; judge the developer's delivery record before accepting it.
Oversupply in a micro-market keeps rents and resale prices flat; months of inventory is the quickest way to measure it.
Exits take months, involve several parties and cost 1% to 2% in brokerage, so plan how you would get money out before buying.
Title, quality, society, interest rate and concentration risks all deserve checks before you commit.

body.text: Case references summarise publicly reported developments and are simplified. Timelines, costs and inventory figures in examples are illustrative. RERA rules and their enforcement vary by state. This lesson is educational and is not legal advice or a recommendation to buy or sell any property.
